clue.text: Belle used to be that woman's cleaner

parts.note: a dish is slang for an attractive person, as a belle is
past tense of 'is'
possessive pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: A gossip remarks that a former beauty is now someone's cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A dishwasher is a machine or person that cleans plates, so it is a kind of cleaner.

clue.text: Event in which Paul's last, he can't do jumps

indicators.note: the letters leap about and land in a new order
last points to the final letter of the preceding name

parts.note: the final letter of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: An athlete called Paul finishes last in a contest because he can't manage the jumping events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' selects the end letter of Paul; 'jumps' looks like the high jump or long jump of the event itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A decathlon is a ten-part athletics competition, a single sporting event on the programme.

clue.text: Quiet European repeated phrase for judge

parts.note: the hushing sound asking for quiet
standard abbreviation
a riff is a short musical phrase played over and over

explanation.surface: Someone describes a quiet European's catchphrase used to address a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland a sheriff is a judge who presides over the local court, which is what makes the definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish sheriff is a judicial officer who tries cases in a sheriff court.

clue.text: Tied to the bed, housework with shackles

indicators.note: to shackle is to bind around, so one piece is clamped on either side of the other

parts.note: 'and' means together with
a chore is a household task

explanation.surface: A kinky scene: someone tied to the bed, doing housework in shackles.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is the seabed, not a bedroom: a ship anchored is held fast to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: An anchored vessel is fastened by its anchor to the seabed, so it is tied to the bed.

clue.text: Fresh roll and if cheese, fresher block

indicators.note: something made fresh is remade, so the letters are formed anew

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A student's lunch order: a fresh roll, and some cheese if there is any.
explanation.walkthrough: A fresher is a first-year university student, and their block is the building they live in.
explanation.definitionFit: A hall of residence is university accommodation, typically the housing block for first-year students.

clue.text: Elaborate golden flip-flops on clown

indicators.note: to flip-flop is to turn round to face the other way

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
Coco was a famous circus clown

explanation.surface: A clown is wearing fancy gold flip-flop sandals.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second. Coco the Clown was a famous Russian-born circus clown in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Rococo is an ornate eighteenth-century decorative style, so the word describes anything highly ornamented.

clue.text: Narrowly defeat second seeds

parts.note: to pip someone is to beat them by a tiny margin
standard abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: In a tennis tournament, a player narrowly beats the second seed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seeds' reads like tournament seedings, but it means fruit pips.
explanation.definitionFit: Pips are the small seeds found inside fruit such as apples and oranges.

clue.text: Tube occasionally seen on the surface, but never underground

definitions.text: Tube occasionally seen on the surface, but never underground

parts.words: Tube occasionally seen on the surface, but never underground
parts.note: surface reading: a London Tube line that sometimes runs above ground but is not an underground railway

parts.words: Tube occasionally seen on the surface
parts.note: setter's reading: a viewing tube from a submarine that pokes above the sea's surface, and is never used underground

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark about a London Tube line that runs above ground and is never underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is London's Underground, so 'never underground' sounds paradoxical; here the tube is an optical one rising above the surface of the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: This optical instrument is a long tube with mirrors that a submerged submarine raises above the water to look around.

clue.text: Average teacher son tolerates

parts.note: par is the normal or average level
a don is a university teacher
standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: An ordinary teacher puts up with a boy's behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: To pardon a fault is to forgive or overlook it, which is to tolerate it.

clue.text: American boards heaving Circle Line for the office

indicators.note: to board is to get on and go inside, as a passenger does a train
heaving means tossing and lurching, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation for line
standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: An American tourist squeezes onto a packed Circle Line train to get to work.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle Line is a London Underground route. The definition is adjectival: clerical work is the work done for an office.
explanation.definitionFit: Clerical describes office work such as filing and typing, the duties of a clerk.

clue.text: Poison not often seen by copper

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
something rare is seldom found

explanation.surface: A detective notes an unusual poison spotted by a police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal's chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Curare is a plant-derived paralysing toxin used by South American hunters on arrow tips.

clue.text: Gaunt muse with potassium deficiency

indicators.note: a deficiency means something is lacking, so that element's symbol is removed

parts.note: to muse is to ponder
K is the chemical symbol for potassium

explanation.surface: A wasted poet's muse looks gaunt from lack of potassium in her diet.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaunt means lean and haggard, which is a strong form of being slender or skinny.

clue.text: Sometimes showing working detains Charlie with calculator

indicators.note: to detain is to hold someone in, so one piece surrounds the following ones

parts.note: a show that is on is being shown
a machine that is on is operating
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
Casio is a well-known maker of pocket calculators

explanation.surface: A maths teacher sometimes keeps Charlie behind for showing his working on a calculator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showing working' looks like maths homework, but each word stands alone; Casio is a calculator brand, a proper name rather than a dictionary word.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means from time to time, now and then, which is a synonym of sometimes.

clue.text: Lords briefly raise swords around king

indicators.note: around means placed on both sides of something
something made brief is cut short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to lift is to raise
épées are fencing swords
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Members of the nobility raise their swords around the monarch in a ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: Life peers are members of the UK House of Lords whose titles cannot be inherited.
explanation.definitionFit: Life peers sit in the House of Lords, so they are lords appointed for their lifetime.

clue.text: Before long home cracks seriously

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one piece pushes inside the other

parts.note: early means ahead of time
a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: A grim prediction that the house will soon start cracking badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnestly means in a sincere, solemn and serious manner, so it is an adverb synonym.

clue.text: Group of boarders posh in stockings

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: hose is an old word for stockings or tights
U means upper-class

explanation.surface: A boarding-school crowd who wear smart stockings.
explanation.walkthrough: In British boarding schools, pupils are split into houses where they live and compete as teams.
explanation.definitionFit: A house in a British boarding school is a residence and team of pupils who board together.

clue.text: Set aside each exam result ringed with red

parts.note: standard abbreviation for each

indicators.note: to be ringed with is to be encircled, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
a mark is a score in an exam

explanation.surface: A teacher puts aside each test where the score has been circled in red ink.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark something is to reserve it for a particular purpose, a synonym of setting it aside.

clue.text: Thanks accepted by parent at home for support

parts.note: Ma is mother
someone at home is in
ta is informal British for thanks
something accepted or fashionable is in

explanation.surface: A grown child at home thanks their parent for continued backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' sets the first pair beside the second, so the parent and home pieces come first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To maintain someone is to provide for them financially, which is to support them.

clue.text: Silver candlestick from the east inlaid with mother-of-pearl

indicators.note: reading from the east in an across clue means reading right to left
something inlaid is set into a surface, so the answer is embedded within the words

parts.note: the letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: An oriental silver candlestick decorated with inlaid mother-of-pearl.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is the iridescent lining of mollusc shells, the material also called mother-of-pearl.

clue.text: Shellfish bachelor tucks into on his own

indicators.note: to tuck into is to slip inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: alone means by oneself
BA, Bachelor of Arts

explanation.surface: A single man eats a seafood dinner on his own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucks into' suggests eating, but here it means slipping inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The abalone is an edible sea mollusc, a type of shellfish with an ear-shaped shell.

clue.text: Big wheels, say, in spinning competition

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
something spinning turns round to face the other way

parts.note: a race is a competition
to state is to say

explanation.surface: A spinning-wheel contest featuring giant wheels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big wheels' is slang for a vehicle; an estate car is the British name for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheels is slang for a car, and an estate car is a large one with an extended rear load space.

clue.text: Walking stick supporting Greek character bends

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so the stick goes below the Greek letter

parts.note: chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a cane is a walking stick

explanation.surface: An elderly Greek man leans on his walking stick and stoops.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, the stick supporting the letter sits beneath it, so it comes second.
explanation.definitionFit: A chicane is a sequence of tight artificial bends on a racing circuit.

clue.text: Sailor on voyage told to come down a rope

parts.note: AB, able seaman

indicators.note: told means spoken out, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a sail is a trip by boat

explanation.surface: A sailor on a trip is ordered to slide down a rope.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second piece is heard rather than read; in British speech the answer is said 'ab-sail'.
explanation.definitionFit: To abseil is to descend a steep face by sliding down a fixed rope.

clue.text: Naughty nurse invited back for afternoon spa

parts.note: naughty means badly behaved
EN, enrolled nurse
bade is the past tense of bid, to invite

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cheeky nurse asks someone round for an afternoon at a health spa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invited back' looks like a phrase, but 'back for afternoon' is the selector. Baden-Baden is a famous German spa town.
explanation.definitionFit: Baden-Baden is a German town famed for its thermal baths, a classic spa resort.

clue.text: Permission to enter when returning after six

parts.note: Roman numeral six

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came

parts.note: as can mean when

explanation.surface: Someone asks permission to come in when they return home after six o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A visa is an official endorsement in a passport allowing the holder into a country.

clue.text: Jack stole bananas for shake

parts.note: J for jack in playing cards

indicators.note: going bananas is going crazy, so the letters run wild

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Jack pinched some bananas to make a milkshake.
explanation.definitionFit: To jostle is to push and shove roughly, which shakes people about.

clue.text: Ship alone on the sea? Wrong, I see a small island

parts.note: 'no' is the reply to a wrong statement
ah is an exclamation of understanding
Sark is one of the smaller Channel Islands

explanation.surface: A lookout reports a lone ship, then corrects himself: it is actually a small island.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: during the Flood this vessel was the only one afloat.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the ark was the sole boat on the floodwaters covering the whole earth.

clue.text: Bank, see, by river

parts.note: standard abbreviation for river
Ely is a cathedral city, and a see is a bishop's diocese

explanation.surface: A tourist points out a riverbank that can be seen by the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like a riverside but is the verb, as in bank on.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to depend on them, the same verb as rely.

clue.text: Distorting life, needle in Tommy's arm

indicators.note: distorting means twisting out of shape, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier's life is warped by an injection needle in his arm.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy is slang for a British soldier, and 'arm' is a weapon, not a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lee-Enfield was the standard British army rifle of both World Wars, the weapon of the ordinary soldier.
